source.title: Random Matrix Theory for Deep Learning: Beyond Eigenvalues of Linear Models [Special Issue on the Mathematics of Deep Learning]

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses RMT analysis and illustrative simulations, rather than the original methods, to report double-descent results for linear regression and single-hidden-layer neural networks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-risk results against sample-size ratio for linear regression and against width for single-hidden-layer networks. It also compares regularization levels. In-sample risks and the gradient-flow discussion do not report an epoch-wise test-error curve. The paper's cited findings from other works are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: This is a tutorial overview of random matrix theory, but it reports its own derivations and simulations (Figs 5b, 6b) of test risk crossing the interpolation point. Ridgeless linear regression is swept over n/p and a random-features network over d/n. These results bear on V3, V4 and V6. Its double-descent results restate known theory rather than introduce new experiments, so the evidence is weak.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors conclude their framework characterizes training and generalization of linear, shallow and deep networks, capturing scaling laws, double descent and learning dynamics. However, double descent is shown only for ridgeless linear regression (over n/p) and the random-features model (over d/n). The deep-network section only linearizes conjugate and neural tangent kernels and reports no double-descent result.
record.recipe_differences: The paper presents an RMT-based overview and asymptotic analysis, with illustrative simulations; it does not reproduce the original study's method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported linear-regression double descent is significantly mitigated by larger regularization (γ = 10^-1 versus γ = 10^-5).
record.problems: The numerical illustrations report averages over 30 runs but no error bars or other uncertainty measures. The empirical settings are limited; several broader claims are asymptotic theoretical results rather than empirical sweeps.
record.rows_left_out: In-sample risk plots and training-dynamics equations were left out because they do not report the claimed test-error curves over size, epochs, or sample count.

untested.parts: No deep or trained multi-layer network width sweep; the deep-network section only linearizes conjugate and neural tangent kernels.
No test error over training time; gradient flow is given as equations only.
Only linear regression on Gaussian data; no neural networks.
Only linear regression and random features; the classical-regime comparison is not framed as a U-curve.
Label-noise dependence, multiple or triple descent, and optimally tuned regularization removing the peak.

missing.what: Closed-form ridgeless out-of-sample risk with divergence at c=p/n=1, contrasted with the classical regime where risk decreases monotonically with n
γ=10^-1 test-MSE curve for the random-features model (empirical and theory) versus γ=10^-5

record.verdict_notes: Overview or tutorial paper (IEEE Signal Processing Magazine) whose double-descent results restate prior theory (Hastie et al.; Mei & Montanari; Liao et al. 2020). The figures are illustrative, averaged over 30 runs, with no error bars. I downweighted the evidence accordingly. R5 should be removed. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The width sweep is for a single-hidden-layer network, not a deep network.
No test-error curve over training epochs is reported.
The reported sample-size result is for ridgeless linear regression; no sample-size sweep is reported for deep networks.
The capacity sweep is for a single-hidden-layer network, not multiple model classes.
The paper does not test whether a single effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.

The paper compares regularization levels and reports mitigation, but does not test whether label noise or variance drives the peak, multiple or triple descent, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The paper does not re-express the curve using an effective parameter count.

rows.subject: ridgeless linear regression β0
rows.operation_detail: Varied the training-sample to dimension ratio n/p and measured out-of-sample risk.

conditions.value: Gaussian x ∼ N(0, Ip), ε ∼ N(0, σ² = 0.1)

rows.value: figure only; text says risk decreases then increases as n approaches p in the n < p regime, reaches a singular peak at n = p, and decreases again for n > p.
rows.note: The numerical curve is shown in Figure 5b; the accompanying text explicitly describes its fall-rise-fall shape.
rows.check: Drop V6. R1 is the near-ridgeless (γ=10^-5) curve, which says nothing about noise driving the peak, multiple peaks, or regularization removing it. The sweep is over samples (n/p at fixed p=512), so it bears on V3, not on a capacity axis.

rows.subject: linear regressor βγ
rows.operation_detail: Varied the training-sample to dimension ratio n/p and measured out-of-sample risk.

conditions.value: Gaussian x ∼ N(0, Ip), ε ∼ N(0, σ² = 0.1)

rows.baseline: γ = 10^-5 is also shown in Figure 5b.
rows.value: figure only; text says the double-descent effect is significantly mitigated for γ = 10^-1.
rows.note: The paper reports mitigation, not disappearance, of the effect at this regularization level.
rows.check: Drop V3: the text only says the peak is 'significantly mitigated' at γ=10^-1. It does not say whether more data still hurts there, and the figure cannot be read. For V6 the peak is reduced but not reported gone, and γ=10^-1 is not stated to be optimally tuned.

conditions.value: the text says the singularity applies regardless of activation function
test data generally differ sufficiently from training data

rows.value: the test risk has a singularity at n/d = 1 as γ → 0; the text says this mirrors double descent.
rows.note: This is an asymptotic statement about a single-hidden-layer network, not a deep network.
rows.check: Drop V6. The subject is really a random-features model: the first-layer W is random and only the readout β is trained, not a trained shallow NN. The result is an asymptotic theoretical singularity at n/d=1 as γ→0, derived from prior work [29]; it is not a measured curve.

relationships.condition: ridgeless/near-ridgeless linear regression (γ=10^-5), Gaussian data, p=512
relationships.reason: R1: per the text, out-of-sample risk rises as n approaches p, peaks at n=p, then falls; the authors say more data paradoxically worsens generalization there.
relationships.display_finding: Out-of-sample risk rises as n approaches p, peaks at n=p, and then falls.

relationships.condition: random-features single-hidden-layer model, asymptotic theory, γ→0, test data differing from training data
relationships.reason: R3: the derived test risk has a singularity at n/d=1, which the authors say mirrors double descent, regardless of activation.
relationships.display_finding: The derived test risk had a singularity at n/d = 1 regardless of activation, which the authors interpreted as mirroring double descent.

relationships.reason: R2: larger ridge regularization 'significantly mitigates' the peak, consistent with regularization suppressing it. Complete removal under optimal tuning is not shown.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing ridge regularization from γ=10^-5 to γ=10^-1 substantially reduced the peak, without establishing complete removal.
